copies/dp: In data parallelism, every GPU keeps a full copy of the training state: the 16-bit weights and gradients, and Adam's 32-bit master copy, m and v. Sixteen bytes per parameter, on every GPU.
copies/waste: A 7 billion parameter model on four GPUs is 112 gigabytes on each: four identical copies.
copies/idea: Sharding keeps just one copy, spread out: each GPU holds a quarter of it. That is the idea of ZeRO, for zero redundancy.
stages/s1: Stage one shards the optimizer state, the twelve bytes of master copy, m and v. Each GPU updates only its own quarter of the weights.
stages/s1n: Per GPU, that is four bytes, plus twelve over four, per parameter: forty nine gigabytes instead of 112.
stages/s2: Stage two shards the gradients too: each GPU only needs the averaged gradient for its own quarter. That makes thirty eight and a half gigabytes.
stages/s3: Stage three shards the weights as well. Everything is split: sixteen N over G, twenty eight gigabytes each.
cost/gather: The price is traffic. With the weights sharded, each piece of them is gathered from the other GPUs just before it is used, then dropped again.
cost/same: The training itself does not change: the same averaged gradient, and the same step, as plain data parallelism. Only where the numbers live.
cost/more: And the memory per GPU keeps falling as GPUs are added: on sixty four of them, the 7 billion parameter model needs one point seven five gigabytes each.
